data.text/markdown:
Age, sex, and borrowing strength

Review the classification API, then revisit a published experiment. A separate logistic regression at every age and sex is flexible, but the data at each node can be scarce. A graph encourages adjacent ages to share information while retaining differences supported by observations. The default is a small, seeded, synthetic adaptation. It runs offline and contains no patient records. The original-data preset implements the statistical method in Tuck, Barratt & Boyd (2021), §5.1, pp.18–19, with verified UCI data and five folds. Its results are computed here; published numbers are reference evidence, never substituted for a run.

data.text/html: Changing the original-data controls does not launch the full experiment until you press Run.
240 observations · 2 covariates · 24 strata. Age and sex select coefficients; they are not duplicated as regressors.

data.text/markdown:
The recipe makes the modeling choices visible

Each model receives the same training observations and fold assignments. Common has one coefficient vector. Separate has age × sex vectors with no graph penalty. Stratified adds an age path and a single sex edge. Graph smoothing includes the intercept. The explicit mask control includes it in local L2 by default, giving a finite local optimum even when a node's observed outcomes all belong to one class. The paper does not explicitly resolve this classification mask; switch it off to measure that sensitivity. The house-price experiment explicitly excludes it. Standardize is a recipe, not a pre-fitted object: every call to fit learns its mean and population variance from that training fold. Original-data categorical domains are declared explicitly. The outcome and the leaking diagnosis method column never enter the feature list. The paper uses summed logistic loss. This package uses its global mean, so a published penalty weight becomes weight / n_train, separately in every fold. Both L2 and graph penalties use the same one-half convention as the paper.
